observation: Cloud providers offer spot instances at typically 3–10× cheaper prices than on-demand instances, but spot instances are preemptible and their availability is highly volatile, varying strongly across zones and over time; availability can change from 100% to 0% within hours. Many workloads accept this uncertainty by checkpointing or re-executing, yet deadline-sensitive applications—such as incorporating new user data into an AI recommendation model or making timely trading decisions—cannot tolerate spot preemptions and therefore rely on expensive on-demand instances, trading cost for predictability. Thus it was unclear how deadline-bound jobs could safely exploit cheap spot resources without missing their deadlines.

claims: Empirical studies of cloud spot markets show that spot prices fluctuate substantially over time and can be far below on-demand prices.
A detailed empirical study of a major cloud provider's spot mechanism shows that spot pricing is not generated by a continuous open auction but follows provider-side pricing behavior.

works.title: Deconstructing Amazon EC2 Spot Instance Pricing

claims: Transparent checkpointing has long been proposed as a mechanism for making long-running computations recoverable from crashes and processor reclaims.
Such checkpoint-based resilience lets a preempted job resume from the last checkpoint, but it does not by itself provide any guarantee that the job will finish before an externally imposed deadline.

works.title: DMTCP: Transparent Checkpointing for Cluster Computations and the Desktop

claims: Production datacenter schedulers use preemption for differentiated resource guarantees: lower-priority batch tasks are evicted when higher-priority, latency-critical services need capacity.
In this model, jobs that require a hard completion or latency target are placed in guaranteed classes that are protected from preemption rather than on preemptible best-effort resources.

claims: Recent preemptible-instance serving systems for AI inference move preemption handling into the application runtime, for example by monitoring impending revocation and migrating model state to another spot instance.
These application-specific mechanisms make latency-sensitive workloads feasible on spot capacity, but they require tight coupling between the workload and the fault-tolerance scheme.
